title: From brainwaves to robotic hands
subtitle: How I built an EEG-to-prosthetic control interface — turning raw neural signals into a graph-neural-network model that drives a robotic hand.
author: Caleb Liu
intro: Raw EEG recordings are messy — muscle artifacts, electrical noise, and overlapping signals all mixed together. The goal was to extract the specific motor-cortex intent needed to control a robotic prosthetic hand, and to do it reliably enough to be useful outside the lab.

sections.label: Neural intent → robotic hand
sections.caption: A graph neural network reads motor-cortex signals and drives a robotic hand in a closed loop.

sections.label: The approach
sections.body: I built an AI mechanical-code bridge: a feature-extraction pipeline that isolates the relevant neural signals, feeding them into a graph neural network that maps neural intent onto robotic hand movements.

sections.label: The approach
sections.body: The key was treating the data as the hard part — cleaning, annotating, and validating the recordings before modeling, so the network learned real intent rather than noise.

sections.label: Feature extraction
sections.caption: Feature-extraction pipeline isolating motor-cortex signals from noisy EEG channels.

sections.label: The result
sections.body: The interface translates neural intent into robotic hand movements with enough fidelity to demonstrate closed-loop control — the hand responds to the user's intent, not just their physical motion.

sections.body: This is the kind of work that pairs brain-computer interfaces with assistive robotics to restore agency for people who need it.
